clinicalPearls: A congenital anomaly in which the urethral meatus opens on the dorsal (upper) surface of the penis in boys or between a bifid clitoris in girls, representing the mildest end of the exstrophy-epispadias complex

In males it is classified by meatal position as glanular, penile, or penopubic; the more proximal (penopubic) the defect, the greater the likelihood of associated sphincteric incompetence and incontinence
The penis is typically short and broad with dorsal chordee (upward curvature)
Continence depends on the integrity of the bladder neck and sphincter, which are more commonly deficient in proximal epispadias
Pubic diastasis of a lesser degree than in exstrophy may be present, reflecting the shared developmental spectrum
It must be distinguished from hypospadias, in which the meatus lies on the ventral surface
Management is surgical reconstruction to reposition the meatus, correct chordee, and, when needed, bladder neck reconstruction to achieve continence
reference.pathophysiology: Epispadias arises from an abnormality of early cloacal and genital tubercle development within the exstrophy-epispadias spectrum, in which the developing genital structures form more caudally than normal, so the urethral plate ends up on the dorsal aspect of the phallus. Depending on the extent of the developmental disturbance, the defect ranges from a distal glanular opening to a proximal penopubic opening with an incompetent bladder neck and sphincter mechanism, and there may be associated separation of the pubic symphysis. The dorsal position of the urethral plate and abnormal corporal development produce the characteristic dorsal chordee and foreshortened penis.
additionalDifferentials: Buried or webbed penis with abnormal meatal appearance
Female urethral or clitoral duplication anomalies
Ambiguous genitalia from a disorder of sex development
Isolated dorsal chordee without meatal abnormality
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination to define meatal position, chordee, and continence
Renal and bladder ultrasound to assess the upper tracts
Micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG) to evaluate reflux and bladder neck
Pelvic imaging to assess pubic diastasis for surgical planning
Urodynamic assessment where continence is in question
Assessment for other associated anomalies of the complex
redFlags: Urinary incontinence indicating a deficient bladder neck or sphincter
Associated upper-tract dilatation or reflux with infection
Features suggesting a more severe exstrophy variant
Ambiguity of the genitalia requiring evaluation for a disorder of sex development
reference.prognosis: Distal epispadias generally has an excellent functional and cosmetic outcome after reconstruction, whereas proximal (penopubic) forms more often require additional bladder neck surgery for continence and may need staged procedures, with fertility and sexual function requiring long-term attention.
pitfalls: Confusing epispadias with hypospadias and mis-planning the repair
Underestimating sphincteric incompetence in proximal defects, leading to persistent incontinence
Failing to recognise membership of the wider exstrophy-epispadias complex
management: Undertake surgical reconstruction as the mainstay, with urethroplasty, correction of dorsal chordee and penile lengthening, typically by a modified Cantwell-Ransley or comparable technique, staged in more proximal defects
Perform bladder neck reconstruction to achieve continence in penopubic forms with sphincteric incompetence
Assess and protect the upper urinary tracts, managing any vesicoureteric reflux identified on imaging
Guide continence care with urodynamic assessment where continence is in doubt
Provide long-term follow-up for continence, sexual function and fertility, supported by a paediatric urology multidisciplinary team
Offer psychological support to the child and family across the reconstructive pathway
